title: Robbie Case: Executive Control Structures

html:
Robbie Case’s Theory of Executive Control Structures is effectively a computational refactoring of Piaget. Where Piaget described what children can do at different stages (the phenomenology), Case provides the system architecture explaining why those limits exist and how transitions occur. A 2026 preschool study models executive function (Figure) 3.

Case explicitly models cognitive development as a resource-constrained optimization problem, positing that the brain’s "hardware" (working memory capacity) remains relatively constant, but "software efficiency" (processing speed/automatization) improves, freeing up space for more complex algorithms.

Case’s fundamental insight is the trade-off between Operating Space (OS; resources required to execute an operation) and Short-Term Storage Space (STSS; resources for holding intermediate results). Total processing space (TPS; fixed biological limit of working memory (the "M-space")) is relatively fixed at any developmental point, but the ratio between OS and STSS shifts with development.

The Equation: TPS=OS+STSSTPS = OS + STSS

The Mechanism: When a new operation (like counting or rotating an object) is learned, it is inefficient and consumes nearly all TPSTPS as OSOS due to a need to simulate/analogize. As the agent practices, structural and synaptic plasticity make the operation efficient (automatization). OSOS requirements drop, freeing up STSSSTSS.

This freed-up storage space allows the agent to hold the results of previous operations in memory while executing new ones, enabling the coordination of multiple variables. A longitudinal study relates motor and executive development (Figure) 4.

He essentially argued that the brain cannot reach higher levels of reasoning until lower-level primitives are compressed enough to run in the background without consuming the mental workspace.

Case replaces the vague Piagetian "schema" with the Executive Control Structure (ECS), which is essentially a mental program or policy. An experiment studies exploration in four-year-olds (Figure) 5.

An ECS always has three components:

Problem Representation: A model of the current state ("I am hungry," "The blocks are uneven").

Objective: A representation of the desired future state ("I want food," "The blocks should be level").

Strategy: The sequence of operations (strategy) to bridge the gap ("Cry," "Add a block to the left").

Practice doesn’t just add "knowledge"; it compiles parts of an ECS into more automatic routines, which frees working-memory resources so the child can assemble a higher-order ECS on top.

Case identifies four major recursive stages. Each stage involves a qualitatively different type of mental "unit" that can be manipulated in working memory.

Stage 1: Sensorimotor (0-1.5 years): The unit is sensory input & motor action.

The world model links inputs to physical outputs (e.g., "Visual of toy" →\rightarrow "Reach arm").

Stage 2: Interrelational (1.5-5 years): The unit is relationships between sensorimotor units.

The world model links actions to outcomes or objects to objects (e.g., "If I push the ball, it rolls away" or "The big block is heavier than the small block").

Stage 3: Dimensional (5-11 years): The unit is dimensions (quantitative variables).

The world model extracts abstract variables from relations (e.g., height, weight, volume, number) and performs operations on them. The child can now model the world using "mental number lines." A developmental study compares numerical and spatial magnitudes (Figure) 6.

Stage 4: Vectorial (11-19 years): The unit is vectors (coordination of multiple dimensions; abstract variables).

The world model represents complex systems where multiple variables interact (e.g., ratios, proportions, trade-offs). This enables second-order abstract thinking (reasoning about the relationship between weight and distance in a balance beam, or on the BMI scale).

Abstract variables (e.g BMI) are often relationships between concrete variables (e.g height and weight), but can also be relationships between other abstract variables (e.g democracy); adult-level cognition involves the hierarchical stacking of dimensions

When you relate two non-concrete (abstract) variables, you create a second-order abstract variable. In systems engineering, we often call these "derivatives," "efficiencies," or "system dynamics." Examples:

Physics: "Power" (the rate of doing work)

To understand "Power" (e.g., horsepower or watts), you must already have "Work" and "Time" as stable concepts. But "Work" itself is already an abstract variable derived from "Force" and "Distance." A developmental experiment tests reasoning about physical variables (Figure) 7.

Level 1 (Concrete):

Mass (mm), Distance (dd), Time (tt).

Level 2 (First-Order Abstract):

Acceleration (aa): A relationship between Velocity and Time.

Force (FF): A relationship between Mass and Acceleration (3F=maF=ma).

Level 3 (Second-Order Abstract):

Work (WW): A relationship between Force and Distance (5W=F⋅dW = F \cdot d).

Level 4 (Relationship between Non-Concretes):

Power (PP): A relationship between Work (Abstract) and Time (Concrete/Abstract); P=WtP = \frac{W}{t}

A child cannot understand "Power" intuitively because to hold it in working memory, they must compress "F⋅dF \cdot d" into a single token "WW". If they have to mentally calculate Force and Distance every time they think about Work, they run out of RAM before they can divide by Time.

Social Cognition: "Equity" (or Fairness)

This is the classic example in developmental psychology. A child (Dimensional stage) thinks "Fairness" means "everyone gets the same amount" (equality of outcome). A fairness study examines children’s responses to unequal outcomes (Figure) 8.

An adult (Vectorial stage) models Equity, which is a comparison of two ratios.

Abstract Variable A (My Deal): The ratio of my Inputs (effort, time, skill) to my Outputs (salary, praise); Rme=InputsmeOutputsmeR_{me} = \frac{Inputs_{me}}{Outputs_{me}}

Abstract Variable B (Your Deal): The ratio of your Inputs to your Outputs; Ryou=InputsyouOutputsyouR_{you} = \frac{Inputs_{you}}{Outputs_{you}}

The Target Variable (Equity): The relationship between these two abstract ratios; Equity⇔Rme≈RyouEquity \iff R_{me} \approx R_{you}

If I work hard and get paid $50, and you do nothing and get paid $50, a child sees "Equality" (50=50 =50). An adult sees "Inequity" because the ratios do not match. You cannot perceive this form of injustice unless your brain can treat "Input/Output Ratio" as a single, manipulable variable.

Economics: "Inflation-Adjusted Return" (Real Rate of Return)

This is a critical concept for long-horizon planning.

Abstract Variable A (Nominal Return): The percentage growth of your money (e.g., 7%). This is already a relation between Principal and Interest.

Abstract Variable B (Inflation): The percentage loss of purchasing power (e.g., 3%). This is a relation between Price Index and Time.

The Target Variable (Real Return): The relationship between Nominal Return and Inflation; Rreal≈Rnominal−RinflationR_{real} \approx R_{nominal} - R_{inflation}

Case observed that within each of the four main stages, the agent goes through the same four-step sub-cycle. This creates a fractal-like developmental pattern where the same coordination process repeats at each level of abstraction.

Substages

Substage 0: Operational Consolidation: The agent can use the new structure, but only in isolation; single unit of new type (e.g., can count, but can’t count and sum).

Substage 1: Unifocal Coordination: The agent can apply the new operation to a single variable at a time. A study examines how young children control variables (Figure).

Substage 2: Bifocal Coordination: The agent can coordinate two units simultaneously (e.g., comparing the height of two beakers).

Substage 3: Elaborated Coordination: The agent can coordinate two or more units in a complex, integrated system. This complex structure then becomes the "single unit" of the next major stage.

Example 1 (the skill of "drawing a scene" across the Dimensional stage of development):

Context: The child has just finished the Relational stage (ages 3-5), meaning they can already draw symbols that represent objects (a circle for a head, lines for legs). Now, they must learn to organize these objects in space. A study examines how children draw and recognize objects (Figure) 9.

Substage 0: Operational Consolidation (approx. age 5-6)

The State: The new capability (representing a dimension/axis) is present but consumes all working memory. The child can focus on the shape of the object or the location, but not both simultaneously in a system.

The Behavior: The child draws a "floating" picture. They draw a house, a person, and a tree. The objects are recognizable, but they are scattered randomly on the page. There is no "ground" and no "up/down" alignment relative to the paper. The drawing study presents annotated examples (Figure).

The Limit: They are running a "Shape" subroutine. When that finishes, they move their hand to a random empty spot and run the next "Shape" subroutine. They cannot hold the global coordinate frame in RAM while drawing the local object.

"Recognizable forms" and "floating objects" between 3.5-7 1

Substage 1: Unifocal Coordination (approx. age 6-7)

The State: The "Shape" subroutine is now efficient enough that the child has spare RAM to pay attention to one spatial dimension (usually the vertical axis).

The Behavior: The "Ground Line" appears. The child draws a green line at the bottom of the page. The house, the tree, and the person all stand perfectly on this line. The study measures inclusion of object parts across ages (Figure).

The Limit: The coordination is Unifocal (one-focus). They can map Object→VerticalPositionObject \rightarrow Vertical Position. However, they cannot handle depth. If they want to draw a house behind the person, they can’t. They usually just put them side-by-side on the single line.

"Development of a baseline" between 5-9 2

Substage 2: Bifocal Coordination (approx. age 8-9)

The State: The child can now coordinate two distinct spatial variables simultaneously. They can handle the vertical axis (up/down) and a second axis (near/far or foreground/background), but they process them as separate steps.

The Behavior: The "Two-Line" drawing. The child draws a ground line at the bottom (foreground) with a person on it. They draw a second ground line higher up (background) with a house on it.

The Conflict: The scene is "bifocal"-it has two distinct focal planes that don’t quite merge. The space in between the two lines is empty/undefined. They know "up on paper = further away," but they can’t create a unified gradient.

"Attempt at depth" between 8-12 2

Substage 3: Elaborated Coordination (approx. age 10)

The State: The two dimensions (vertical and depth) are integrated into a single coherent system. This system (a 2D coordinate plane) becomes the "unit" for the next stage.

The Behavior: Integrated perspective. The child draws a scene with a continuous ground plane (e.g., a road receding into the distance). They use occlusion (the person blocks part of the house) to show depth.

"Awareness of depth" between ages 11-14 2

The Transition: This "Elaborated" structure-a fully integrated 3D-to-2D mapping-is now a "solid block" of logic. In the next major stage (Vectorial, ages 11-18), they will take this entire block and treat it as merely one "unit" to be manipulated (e.g., in mechanical drawing, where they must coordinate multiple 3D views-top, side, front-of the same object).

Example 2 (understanding a basic narrative across the "Interrelational" stage of development (age 1.5-5)):

The "unit" that serves as the input of this stage is a Relationship (Cause →\rightarrow Effect). The longitudinal study models relationships among cognitive measures (Figure).

Substage 0 (Consolidation): The child can enact a script but can’t modify it. They can play "Mommy feeds baby." If you interrupt the script, they get confused and have to start over.

Substage 1 (Unifocal): Focus on one relationship change. "The baby is crying because she is hungry." (One Cause →\rightarrow One Effect).

Substage 2 (Bifocal): Coordinating two relationships, often in a chain. "The baby is crying because she is hungry, so Mommy cooks food." (A →\rightarrow B, and B →\rightarrow C).

Substage 3 (Elaborated): Integrated relationship system. "Mommy is cooking food, but the baby is still crying because the food is too hot."

The child is integrating a positive leg (cooking fixes hunger) and a negative leg (heat prevents eating) into a single mental model of the situation.

If you want an agent to understand "Elaborated" logic (Level 3), you must force it to:

1. Master the isolated tool (Level 0). 2. Apply it to single variables until the compute cost drops (Level 1). 3. Apply it to conflicting variables in parallel (Level 2). 4. Only then will the agent have the "spare RAM" to derive the integration rule (Level 3).

General algorithm: consolidate -> coordinate pairs -> integrate -> treat as primitive for next level

While Piaget looked for "general" logic, Case recognized that efficiency gains are often domain-specific. He proposed Central Conceptual Structures (CCS): semantic networks that form the "core knowledge" for specific domains; in his words, "networks of semantic notes and relations that have an extremely broad (but not system-wide) domain of application and that are central to children’s functioning in that domain."

Examples:

Numerical CCS: A mental number line (linking quantity, numeral, and order); concepts: more/less, addition, relative magnitude

Narrative CCS: A schema for human action (agent, intention, obstacle, resolution); concepts: intention, desire, action sequences, emotional states

Spatial CCS: A coordinate system for object location and movement; concepts: position, direction, distance

A child might be at the "Vectorial" stage in Narrative (understanding complex social motivations) but still at the "Dimensional" stage in Number, depending on where they have applied their processing efficiency. CCS are modular; they are, however, interconnected: they develop somewhat independently but can be coordinated for cross-domain reasoning (e.g., using number concepts to reason about space or agents). The exploration study examines differences between children (Figure).

Developmental mechanisms (which are related):

Biological Maturation: increased neural myelination -> faster processing

Practice & Automatization: reduced operating space demands -> freed capacity

Hierarchical Integration: chunking coordinated structures into single units
